content:
## Two things to settle before the code

**1. `s3.aws.upbound.io` is not ACK.** The task says "Use ACK S3 CRDs (`s3.aws.upbound.io`)" — those are two different products:

| | API group | Model |
|---|---|---|
| **ACK** (AWS Controllers for Kubernetes) | `s3.services.k8s.aws/v1alpha1` | One `Bucket` CR with `versioning`/`encryption`/`publicAccessBlock` as inline sub-fields |
| **Crossplane / Upbound provider-aws** | `s3.aws.upbound.io/v1beta1..2` | Separate MRs: `Bucket`, `BucketVersioning`, `BucketServerSideEncryptionConfiguration`, `BucketPublicAccessBlock`, plus `providerConfigRef` |

The stack description and the task title both say ACK, so **I've written the primary implementation against ACK** and put the Upbound/Crossplane equivalent in an appendix. Run `kubectl api-resources | grep -iE 's3\.(services\.k8s\.aws|aws\.upbound\.io)'` to confirm which is actually installed before applying.

**2. There is nothing to SOPS-encrypt here.** Bucket names, IAM role ARNs, AWS account IDs and EKS OIDC provider IDs are not secrets — they're all discoverable from any authenticated session and appear in plaintext CloudTrail. Encrypting them adds a key-rotation burden with zero confidentiality gain, and it breaks `kustomize build` for reviewers. In the canonical scenario the SOPS-encrypted item is the **DB connection string**, which this change doesn't touch. I've left a commented-out `decryption` block on the Flux Kustomizations so it's one line to enable if you later add an encrypted file under these paths.

**Also: the context files weren't attached.** Only the scenario spec came through — I don't have `flux/kustomizations.yaml`, the existing `infra/s3/`, or the overlay roots. Everything below marked 🔧 is a placeholder you must reconcile with the real repo.

---

## Assumptions (🔧 = verify/replace)

| Item | Assumed | 
|---|---|
| 🔧 Flux source | `GitRepository/flux-system` in ns `flux-system` |
| 🔧 App namespace | `myapp` (dev and prod on **separate clusters**) |
| 🔧 ACK controllers installed | `s3` + `iam`, watching ns `myapp` |
| 🔧 Regions | dev `us-east-2`, prod `us-east-1` (prod replicates *to* us-west-2 per spec, so it can't be primary there) |
| 🔧 AWS account IDs | dev `111111111111`, prod `222222222222` |
| 🔧 EKS OIDC provider IDs | `EXAMPLEDEV0123456789` / `EXAMPLEPRD0123456789` |
| 🔧 Flux version | ≥ v2.4 (needed for `healthCheckExprs`) |
| Bucket names | `myapp-logs-dev` / `myapp-logs-prod` — **see gotcha #2, these are almost certainly already taken globally** |

---

## File tree

```
infra/
  s3/logs/
    kustomization.yaml
    bucket.yaml
  iam/logs/
    kustomization.yaml
    role.yaml
    serviceaccount.yaml
overlays/
  dev/logs/
    kustomization.yaml
    patch-bucket.yaml
    patch-role.yaml
    patch-serviceaccount.yaml
  prod/logs/
    (same four files)
flux/
  kustomizations.yaml        # append 2 documents
```

Bucket lives under `infra/s3/`, role under `infra/iam/` to match your existing split; the overlay composes both so they ship as one unit.

---

## Base: `infra/s3/logs/`

**`infra/s3/logs/bucket.yaml`**
```yaml
apiVersion: s3.services.k8s.aws/v1alpha1
kind: Bucket
metadata:
  name: myapp-logs
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: myapp
    app.kubernetes.io/component: logs
  annotations:
    # Flux prune / manifest removal deletes the CR but leaves the AWS bucket.
    # Requires ACK runtime >= v0.20 — drop this line on older controllers.
    services.k8s.aws/deletion-policy: retain
spec:
  # spec.name is the real AWS bucket name; overridden per environment.
  name: myapp-logs
  # Disables ACLs entirely. Do NOT also set spec.acl — they conflict.
  ownershipControls:
    rules:
      - objectOwnership: BucketOwnerEnforced
  # Requirement 4: no public access
  publicAccessBlock:
    blockPublicACLs: true
    blockPublicPolicy: true
    ignorePublicACLs: true
    restrictPublicBuckets: true
  # Requirement 2: versioning
  versioning:
    status: Enabled
  # Requirement 3: SSE-AES256
  encryption:
    rules:
      - applyServerSideEncryptionByDefault:
          sseAlgorithm: AES256
        bucketKeyEnabled: true
  tagging:
    tagSet:
      - key: app
        value: myapp
      - key: component
        value: logs
      - key: managed-by
        value: ack
```

**`infra/s3/logs/kustomization.yaml`**
```yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
  - bucket.yaml
```

---

## Base: `infra/iam/logs/`

**`infra/iam/logs/role.yaml`**
```yaml
apiVersion: iam.services.k8s.aws/v1alpha1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: myapp-logs-writer
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: myapp
    app.kubernetes.io/component: logs
spec:
  name: myapp-logs-writer
  description: IRSA role granting read/write on the myapp logs bucket
  maxSessionDuration: 3600
  # PLACEHOLDER — fully replaced by every overlay. Intentionally unusable
  # so a stray `kubectl apply -k infra/iam/logs` cannot create a real trust.
  assumeRolePolicyDocument: |
    {
      "Version": "2012-10-17",
      "Statement": [
        {
          "Effect": "Deny",
          "Principal": {"AWS": "*"},
          "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
        }
      ]
    }
  # PLACEHOLDER — replaced per overlay (bucket ARN differs per env).
  inlinePolicies:
    logs-bucket-rw: |
      {"Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": []}
  tags:
    - key: app
      value: myapp
    - key: component
      value: logs
```

**`infra/iam/logs/serviceaccount.yaml`**

The `sub` claim in the trust policy is `system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa-name>` — the role is meaningless without a matching SA, so it ships alongside it.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: myapp-logs
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: myapp
    app.kubernetes.io/component: logs
  annotations:
    # Overridden per overlay with the real account ID.
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::000000000000:role/PLACEHOLDER
```

**`infra/iam/logs/kustomization.yaml`**
```yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
  - role.yaml
  - serviceaccount.yaml
```

---

## Overlay: `overlays/dev/logs/`
